Question:
Show the names of the buildings that have more than one company offices.
answer: SELECT T2.name FROM Office_locations AS T1 JOIN buildings AS T2 ON T1.building_id  =  T2.id JOIN Companies AS T3 ON T1.company_id  =  T3.id GROUP BY T1.building_id HAVING COUNT(*)  >  1

metadata.question: Show the names of the buildings that have more than one company offices.

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from the office-location records, since each row associates a company office with a building: `FROM Office_locations AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join the buildings table to access the name of each building: `FROM Office_locations AS T1 JOIN buildings AS T2 ON T1.building_id  =  T2.id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I also join each office record to its company using the company id: `FROM Office_locations AS T1 JOIN buildings AS T2 ON T1.building_id  =  T2.id JOIN Companies AS T3 ON T1.company_id  =  T3.id`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I group the office records by building and retain buildings associated with more than one row: `FROM Office_locations AS T1 JOIN buildings AS T2 ON T1.building_id  =  T2.id JOIN Companies AS T3 ON T1.company_id  =  T3.id GROUP BY T1.building_id HAVING COUNT(*)  >  1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I select the names of the qualifying buildings: `SELECT T2.name FROM Office_locations AS T1 JOIN buildings AS T2 ON T1.building_id  =  T2.id JOIN Companies AS T3 ON T1.company_id  =  T3.id GROUP BY T1.building_id HAVING COUNT(*)  >  1`.

answer: SELECT t1.name ,  t1.age FROM pilot AS t1 JOIN MATCH AS t2 ON t1.pilot_id  =  t2.winning_pilot ORDER BY t1.age LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_4: I retain only the first row, which gives the youngest winning pilot: `SELECT t1.name ,  t1.age FROM pilot AS t1 JOIN MATCH AS t2 ON t1.pilot_id  =  t2.winning_pilot ORDER BY t1.age LIMIT 1`.

Question:
What is the name of the team that got more wins than loses in the Stanley Cup finals in 1917?

Evidence:
more wins than loses refers to W>L; year = 1917;
answer: SELECT T2.name FROM TeamsSC AS T1 INNER JOIN Teams AS T2 ON T1.tmID = T2.tmID AND T1.year = T2.year WHERE T1.year = '1917' AND T1.W > T1.L

prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the Stanley Cup records to 1917: `FROM TeamsSC AS T1 INNER JOIN Teams AS T2 ON T1.tmID = T2.tmID AND T1.year = T2.year WHERE T1.year = '1917'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I keep the team whose wins exceeded its losses: `FROM TeamsSC AS T1 INNER JOIN Teams AS T2 ON T1.tmID = T2.tmID AND T1.year = T2.year WHERE T1.year = '1917' AND T1.W > T1.L`.

Question:
How many male employees have the job position of sales person?

Evidence:
Sales person refers to PersonType = 'SP'; Male refers to Gender = 'M';
answer: SELECT COUNT(T1.BusinessEntityID) FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.Gender = 'M' AND T2.PersonType = 'SP'

metadata.question: How many male employees have the job position of sales person?
metadata.evidence: Sales person refers to PersonType = 'SP'; Male refers to Gender = 'M';

prefix_hints.sol_1: Employee gender is in `Employee`, so I start from that table: `FROM Employee AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: The sales-person designation is in `Person`, so I join each employee to the matching person record by business entity id: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the joined records to male employees: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.Gender = 'M'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I then keep those whose person type is `SP`, indicating sales person: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.Gender = 'M' AND T2.PersonType = 'SP'`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I count the matching employee business entity ids: `SELECT COUNT(T1.BusinessEntityID) FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.Gender = 'M' AND T2.PersonType = 'SP'`.

DIVIDE(COUNT(PATIENT when DESCRIPTION = 'Influenza seasonal injectable preservative free'), COUNT(PATIENT)) as percentage where strftime('%Y', 2017); English refers ethnicity = 'english';

Question:
What are the names of products that have never been ordered?
answer: SELECT product_name FROM Products EXCEPT SELECT T1.product_name FROM Products AS T1 JOIN Order_items AS T2 ON T1.product_id  =  T2.product_id

metadata.question: What are the names of products that have never been ordered?

prefix_hints.sol_1: I begin with the product names that form the full set of candidates: `SELECT product_name`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I take those candidate names from the Products table: `SELECT product_name FROM Products`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I subtract a second set containing the names of products that appear in orders: `SELECT product_name FROM Products EXCEPT SELECT T1.product_name`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I build that ordered-product set by joining Products to Order_items on product_id: `SELECT product_name FROM Products EXCEPT SELECT T1.product_name FROM Products AS T1 JOIN Order_items AS T2 ON T1.product_id  =  T2.product_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: This set difference returns exactly the products that have never been ordered: `SELECT product_name FROM Products EXCEPT SELECT T1.product_name FROM Products AS T1 JOIN Order_items AS T2 ON T1.product_id  =  T2.product_id`.

Question:
For the planes which has the hightest total price, how much it exceeds the average?

Evidence:
plane is a product line; total price = MULTIPLY(quantityOrdered, priceEach); how much the total price exceeds the average = SUBTRACT(MAX(MULTIPLY(quantityOrdered, priceEach))), AVG(priceEach));
answer: SELECT MAX(quantityOrdered * priceEach) - AVG(priceEach) FROM orderdetails WHERE productCode IN ( SELECT productCode FROM products WHERE productLine = 'Planes' )

prefix_hints.sol_2: I subtract the average unit price to measure how much that maximum exceeds the average: `SELECT MAX(quantityOrdered * priceEach) - AVG(priceEach)`.

prefix_hints.sol_4: I restrict those order details by starting a product-code subquery against the products table: `SELECT MAX(quantityOrdered * priceEach) - AVG(priceEach) FROM orderdetails WHERE productCode IN ( SELECT productCode FROM products`.

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from the drivers table, which contains each driver's id and family name: `FROM drivers AS T1`.

prefix_hints.sol_3: I sort the joined records by milliseconds in descending order, placing the longest lap time first: `FROM drivers AS T1 JOIN laptimes AS T2 ON T1.driverid = T2.driverid ORDER BY T2.milliseconds DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I retain only that first, longest-lap record: `FROM drivers AS T1 JOIN laptimes AS T2 ON T1.driverid = T2.driverid ORDER BY T2.milliseconds DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I project the driver's id and surname from the selected record: `SELECT T1.driverid ,  T1.surname FROM drivers AS T1 JOIN laptimes AS T2 ON T1.driverid = T2.driverid ORDER BY T2.milliseconds DESC LIMIT 1`.

Question:
Among the active businesses in Arizona, how many businesses work after 12PM?

Evidence:
active businesses in Arizona refer to business_id where state = 'Arizona' and active = 'true'; work after 12PM refer to opening_time > '12PM';
answer: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T2.business_id) FROM Business_Hours AS T1 INNER JOIN Business AS T2 ON T1.business_id = T2.business_id INNER JOIN Business_Categories AS T3 ON T2.business_id = T3.business_id INNER JOIN Categories AS T4 ON T3.category_id = T4.category_id WHERE T2.active = 'true' AND T2.state = 'AZ' AND T1.opening_time > '12PM'

prefix_hints.sol_2: I continue through the business-category relationship and join the category records: `FROM Business_Hours AS T1 INNER JOIN Business AS T2 ON T1.business_id = T2.business_id INNER JOIN Business_Categories AS T3 ON T2.business_id = T3.business_id INNER JOIN Categories AS T4 ON T3.category_id = T4.category_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the joined rows to active businesses located in Arizona, represented by the state code AZ: `FROM Business_Hours AS T1 INNER JOIN Business AS T2 ON T1.business_id = T2.business_id INNER JOIN Business_Categories AS T3 ON T2.business_id = T3.business_id INNER JOIN Categories AS T4 ON T3.category_id = T4.category_id WHERE T2.active = 'true' AND T2.state = 'AZ'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I then retain businesses whose opening time is later than 12PM: `FROM Business_Hours AS T1 INNER JOIN Business AS T2 ON T1.business_id = T2.business_id INNER JOIN Business_Categories AS T3 ON T2.business_id = T3.business_id INNER JOIN Categories AS T4 ON T3.category_id = T4.category_id WHERE T2.active = 'true' AND T2.state = 'AZ' AND T1.opening_time > '12PM'`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Because the joins can produce multiple rows for one business, I count distinct business ids to finish the query: `SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T2.business_id) FROM Business_Hours AS T1 INNER JOIN Business AS T2 ON T1.business_id = T2.business_id INNER JOIN Business_Categories AS T3 ON T2.business_id = T3.business_id INNER JOIN Categories AS T4 ON T3.category_id = T4.category_id WHERE T2.active = 'true' AND T2.state = 'AZ' AND T1.opening_time > '12PM'`.

Question:

Arab is the name of enthic groups in the country; Population of (Arab in each country) = (percentage of Arab) * (population of each country)
answer: SELECT T2.Percentage * T1.Population FROM country AS T1 INNER JOIN ethnicGroup AS T2 ON T1.Code = T2.Country WHERE T2.Name = 'Arab'

intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT park FROM team WHERE name = "Washington Nationals" GROUP BY park

intermediate_turns.question: How many players have played for this team?
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T3.name = 'Washington Nationals'

intermediate_turns.question: Could you please list their full names?
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT T2.name_first ,  T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T3.name = 'Washington Nationals' GROUP BY T2.player_id

intermediate_turns.question: How about names of the players that played for this team in both 2005 and 2007
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT T2.name_first ,  T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T1.year = 2005 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals' INTERSECT SELECT T2.name_first , T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T1.year = 2007 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals'

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start the 2005 result set by selecting each salaried player's first and last name from `salary` and joining to `player`: `SELECT T2.name_first ,  T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join the team records through the salary row's team id so I can identify the Washington Nationals: `SELECT T2.name_first ,  T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I complete the first result set by restricting it to 2005 salaries from the Washington Nationals: `SELECT T2.name_first ,  T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T1.year = 2005 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I intersect that result with the same player-and-team lookup for the second year: `SELECT T2.name_first ,  T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T1.year = 2005 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals' INTERSECT SELECT T2.name_first , T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I restrict the intersected result set to Washington Nationals salaries in 2007, leaving only names present in both years: `SELECT T2.name_first ,  T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T1.year = 2005 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals' INTERSECT SELECT T2.name_first , T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T1.year = 2007 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals'`.

prefix_hints.sol_3: I sort the qualifying results by fastest-lap speed from highest to lowest: `FROM drivers AS T1 INNER JOIN results AS T2 ON T2.driverId = T1.driverId WHERE T2.fastestLapTime IS NOT NULL ORDER BY T2.fastestLapSpeed DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I take only the first row, which represents the highest fastest-lap speed: `FROM drivers AS T1 INNER JOIN results AS T2 ON T2.driverId = T1.driverId WHERE T2.fastestLapTime IS NOT NULL ORDER BY T2.fastestLapSpeed DESC LIMIT 1`.

Question:
For all the games ended up with 1-1, what percentage of them are from Liga NOS division?

Evidence:
1-1 is a score where FTHG = '1' and FTAG = '1'; Liga NOS is the name of division; DIVIDE(COUNT(Div where FTHG = '1', FTAG = '1', name = 'Liga NOS'), COUNT(Div where FTHG = '1' and FTAG = '1')) as percentage;
answer: SELECT CAST(COUNT(CASE WHEN T2.name = 'Liga NOS' THEN T1.Div ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T1.Div) FROM matchs AS T1 INNER JOIN divisions AS T2 ON T1.Div = T2.division WHERE T1.FTHG = 1 AND FTAG = 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: I join customers to their transactions on CustomerID so each purchase is associated with the customer's gender: `FROM customers AS T1 INNER JOIN `transaction` AS T2 ON T1.CustomerID = T2.CustomerID`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I keep purchases made by male customers by filtering Gender to M: `FROM customers AS T1 INNER JOIN `transaction` AS T2 ON T1.CustomerID = T2.CustomerID WHERE T1.Gender = 'M'`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the matching purchases by transaction date so each date has its own purchase count: `FROM customers AS T1 INNER JOIN `transaction` AS T2 ON T1.CustomerID = T2.CustomerID WHERE T1.Gender = 'M' GROUP BY T2.TransactionDate`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I retain only dates with more than three matching customer transactions: `FROM customers AS T1 INNER JOIN `transaction` AS T2 ON T1.CustomerID = T2.CustomerID WHERE T1.Gender = 'M' GROUP BY T2.TransactionDate HAVING COUNT(T2.CustomerID) > 3`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I project the qualifying transaction dates, completing the query: `SELECT T2.TransactionDate FROM customers AS T1 INNER JOIN `transaction` AS T2 ON T1.CustomerID = T2.CustomerID WHERE T1.Gender = 'M' GROUP BY T2.TransactionDate HAVING COUNT(T2.CustomerID) > 3`.

Question:
Which Production Technician has the highest pay rate?

Evidence:
highest pay rate refers to MAX(Rate);
answer: SELECT T1.BusinessEntityID FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.JobTitle LIKE 'Production Technician%' ORDER BY T2.Rate DESC LIMIT 1

metadata.question: Which Production Technician has the highest pay rate?
metadata.evidence: highest pay rate refers to MAX(Rate);

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with employees so I can identify each technician by BusinessEntityID and inspect their job title: `FROM Employee AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each employee to their pay history on the shared BusinessEntityID so their rates are available: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I keep job titles beginning with Production Technician to include every technician level: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.JobTitle LIKE 'Production Technician%'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I sort the matching pay-history records by rate in descending order, placing the highest rate first: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.JobTitle LIKE 'Production Technician%' ORDER BY T2.Rate DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I return the BusinessEntityID from that first record and limit the result to one technician: `SELECT T1.BusinessEntityID FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.JobTitle LIKE 'Production Technician%' ORDER BY T2.Rate DESC LIMIT 1`.

metadata.question: What is the order price of the book "The Servant Leader" in 2003?
metadata.evidence: "The Servant Leader" is the title of the book; book in 2003 refers to SUBSTR(publication_date, 1, 4) = '2003'

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from the `book` table, which contains the title and publication date: `FROM book AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join `order_line` by book id so the corresponding order price is available: `FROM book AS T1 INNER JOIN order_line AS T2 ON T1.book_id = T2.book_id`.

prefix_hints.sol_1: I connect each inventory record to its store so I can measure the film collection held by each store: `FROM inventory AS T1 INNER JOIN store AS T2 ON T1.store_id = T2.store_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I then join each store to its manager through `manager_staff_id`: `FROM inventory AS T1 INNER JOIN store AS T2 ON T1.store_id = T2.store_id INNER JOIN staff AS T3 ON T2.manager_staff_id = T3.staff_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the inventory records by manager and count the film ids to obtain each manager's store collection size: `SELECT T3.first_name, T3.last_name, COUNT(T1.film_id) AS num FROM inventory AS T1 INNER JOIN store AS T2 ON T1.store_id = T2.store_id INNER JOIN staff AS T3 ON T2.manager_staff_id = T3.staff_id GROUP BY T3.first_name, T3.last_name`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I place those manager-level counts in a derived table and project the manager's first and last names: `SELECT T.first_name, T.last_name FROM ( SELECT T3.first_name, T3.last_name, COUNT(T1.film_id) AS num FROM inventory AS T1 INNER JOIN store AS T2 ON T1.store_id = T2.store_id INNER JOIN staff AS T3 ON T2.manager_staff_id = T3.staff_id GROUP BY T3.first_name, T3.last_name ) AS T`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I sort the managers by collection size in descending order and keep the largest one: `SELECT T.first_name, T.last_name FROM ( SELECT T3.first_name, T3.last_name, COUNT(T1.film_id) AS num FROM inventory AS T1 INNER JOIN store AS T2 ON T1.store_id = T2.store_id INNER JOIN staff AS T3 ON T2.manager_staff_id = T3.staff_id GROUP BY T3.first_name, T3.last_name ) AS T ORDER BY T.num DESC LIMIT 1`.

answer: SELECT t1.customer_name FROM customers AS t1 JOIN customer_orders AS t2 ON t1.customer_id  =  t2.customer_id JOIN order_items AS t3 ON t2.order_id  =  t3.order_id GROUP BY t1.customer_name ORDER BY sum(t3.order_quantity) DESC LIMIT 1

metadata.question: Give me the name of the customer who ordered the most items in total.

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with customers and connect each customer to their orders through the shared customer id: `FROM customers AS t1 JOIN customer_orders AS t2 ON t1.customer_id  =  t2.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I then connect those orders to their line items so their quantities are available: `FROM customers AS t1 JOIN customer_orders AS t2 ON t1.customer_id  =  t2.customer_id JOIN order_items AS t3 ON t2.order_id  =  t3.order_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the joined rows by customer name so the item quantities can be totaled for each customer: `FROM customers AS t1 JOIN customer_orders AS t2 ON t1.customer_id  =  t2.customer_id JOIN order_items AS t3 ON t2.order_id  =  t3.order_id GROUP BY t1.customer_name`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I rank the customer groups by their summed order quantities in descending order: `FROM customers AS t1 JOIN customer_orders AS t2 ON t1.customer_id  =  t2.customer_id JOIN order_items AS t3 ON t2.order_id  =  t3.order_id GROUP BY t1.customer_name ORDER BY sum(t3.order_quantity) DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I select the customer name and keep only the top-ranked result: `SELECT t1.customer_name FROM customers AS t1 JOIN customer_orders AS t2 ON t1.customer_id  =  t2.customer_id JOIN order_items AS t3 ON t2.order_id  =  t3.order_id GROUP BY t1.customer_name ORDER BY sum(t3.order_quantity) DESC LIMIT 1`.

metadata.question: Find the SSN and name of scientists who are assigned to the project with the longest hours.

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from the assignments and join each one to its project so the recorded hours are available: `FROM assignedto AS T1 JOIN projects AS T2 ON T1.project  =  T2.code`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I then join the assigned scientist to the scientists table to obtain the SSN and name: `FROM assignedto AS T1 JOIN projects AS T2 ON T1.project  =  T2.code JOIN scientists AS T3 ON T1.scientist  =  T3.SSN`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I identify the longest project duration by taking the maximum hours across all projects: `FROM assignedto AS T1 JOIN projects AS T2 ON T1.project  =  T2.code JOIN scientists AS T3 ON T1.scientist  =  T3.SSN WHERE T2.hours  =  (SELECT max(hours) FROM projects)`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I project the SSN and name of every scientist whose assigned project has that maximum duration: `SELECT T3.ssn ,  T3.name FROM assignedto AS T1 JOIN projects AS T2 ON T1.project  =  T2.code JOIN scientists AS T3 ON T1.scientist  =  T3.SSN WHERE T2.hours  =  (SELECT max(hours) FROM projects)`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: This completes the query for scientists assigned to the project with the longest hours: `SELECT T3.ssn ,  T3.name FROM assignedto AS T1 JOIN projects AS T2 ON T1.project  =  T2.code JOIN scientists AS T3 ON T1.scientist  =  T3.SSN WHERE T2.hours  =  (SELECT max(hours) FROM projects)`.

Give the code of sets have expansion type of 'expansion'?

Evidence:
code of sets refers to setCode
answer: SELECT T2.setCode FROM sets AS T1 INNER JOIN set_translations AS T2 ON T2.setCode = T1.code WHERE T1.type = 'expansion' GROUP BY T2.setCode

metadata.question: Give the code of sets have expansion type of 'expansion'?
metadata.evidence: code of sets refers to setCode

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from `sets`, where the set type and canonical code are stored: `FROM sets AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join `set_translations` so I can return the requested `setCode`, matching it to the set's `code`: `FROM sets AS T1 INNER JOIN set_translations AS T2 ON T2.setCode = T1.code`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the matched sets to those whose type is expansion: `FROM sets AS T1 INNER JOIN set_translations AS T2 ON T2.setCode = T1.code WHERE T1.type = 'expansion'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I group by `setCode` so each qualifying set code appears as one group: `FROM sets AS T1 INNER JOIN set_translations AS T2 ON T2.setCode = T1.code WHERE T1.type = 'expansion' GROUP BY T2.setCode`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I project the grouped set codes to complete the query: `SELECT T2.setCode FROM sets AS T1 INNER JOIN set_translations AS T2 ON T2.setCode = T1.code WHERE T1.type = 'expansion' GROUP BY T2.setCode`.

prefix_hints.sol_4: I intersect that result with cities joined to `hosting_city`, retaining only names that have served as host cities: `SELECT T1.city FROM city AS T1 JOIN temperature AS T2 ON T1.city_id  =  T2.city_id WHERE T2.Mar  <  T2.Jul INTERSECT SELECT T3.city FROM city AS T3 JOIN hosting_city AS T4 ON T3.city_id  =  T4.host_city`.

Question:
What is the average quantity of each order for the book "Life Without Fear"?

Evidence:
qty is abbreviation for quantity; average quantity order = AVG(qty)
answer: SELECT CAST(SUM(T2.qty) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.title_id) FROM titles AS T1 INNER JOIN sales AS T2 ON T1.title_id = T2.title_id WHERE T1.title = 'Life Without Fear'

metadata.question: What is the average quantity of each order for the book "Life Without Fear"?
metadata.evidence: qty is abbreviation for quantity; average quantity order = AVG(qty)

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from `titles`, where the requested book is identified: `FROM titles AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join `sales` on the title id so each matching order quantity is available: `FROM titles AS T1 INNER JOIN sales AS T2 ON T1.title_id = T2.title_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the joined rows to the book titled "Life Without Fear": `FROM titles AS T1 INNER JOIN sales AS T2 ON T1.title_id = T2.title_id WHERE T1.title = 'Life Without Fear'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I divide the sum of its order quantities by the number of matching title-order rows, casting the sum to REAL for non-integer division: `SELECT CAST(SUM(T2.qty) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.title_id) FROM titles AS T1 INNER JOIN sales AS T2 ON T1.title_id = T2.title_id WHERE T1.title = 'Life Without Fear'`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: This gives the complete average-quantity query: `SELECT CAST(SUM(T2.qty) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.title_id) FROM titles AS T1 INNER JOIN sales AS T2 ON T1.title_id = T2.title_id WHERE T1.title = 'Life Without Fear'`.

Question:
For the user who gave the most number of long reviews, what is his/her averge ratings of all review?

Evidence:
long reviews refers to review_length = 'long'; most number of long reviews refers to MAX(COUNT(review_length = 'long')); average ratings = AVG(review_stars);
answer: SELECT CAST(SUM(T1.review_stars) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.review_stars) FROM Reviews AS T1 INNER JOIN Users AS T2 ON T1.user_id = T2.user_id WHERE T1.review_length LIKE 'Long' GROUP BY T1.user_id ORDER BY COUNT(T1.review_length) DESC LIMIT 1

metadata.question: For the employee who has been hired the latest, what is his or her pay rate?
metadata.evidence: hired the latest refers to max(HireDate)

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from `EmployeePayHistory`, where each employee's pay rate is stored: `FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1`.
